::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" .lexicon-source}
Entry **#30** in Andrew Gelman's [Handy Statistical Lexicon](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/). Original discussion: [No Bayesians in foxholes](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2006/12/no_bayesians_in/).
:::

## What it is

"There are no atheists in foxholes" claims that under real pressure, everyone comes around to belief. The foxhole fallacy is the general form of the argument: "when it *really* matters, everybody does it my way." In statistics you hear "there are no Bayesians in foxholes," or the reverse, "when the stakes are high, everyone wants a prior." Gelman's post points out how often this rhetorical move appears and how little evidence usually stands behind it.

## Why it matters

The claim is unfalsifiable as usually stated. Anyone who doesn't convert under pressure wasn't in a "real" foxhole. It also rests on anecdote, and on anecdotes filtered by the arguer's own side. People remember the dramatic conversion *toward* their view and forget the quiet cases going the other way. It replaces evidence about what works under pressure with a story about who is serious.

## How it works

A toy model of the evidence behind a foxhole claim. Under pressure, some practitioners switch methods, in both directions, at similar rates. The arguer observes switches through a biased memory: switches toward their view are noticed with high probability and switches away with low probability. Their "evidence" shows a one-way stampede even when the true net flow is zero.

## Simulated example

There are 1,000 practitioners in high-pressure situations. Set the true switching rates in each direction and how selective the arguer's memory is.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof toMine = Inputs.range([0, 0.2], {value: 0.05, step: 0.01, label: "True rate of switching TO my method"})
viewof fromMine = Inputs.range([0, 0.2], {value: 0.05, step: 0.01, label: "True rate of switching AWAY"})
viewof memoryBias = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.8, step: 0.05, label: "Memory selectivity"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
foxhole = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  let toT = 0, fromT = 0, toR = 0, fromR = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    const usesMine = i < 500;
    if (!usesMine && r() < toMine) { toT++; if (r() < 0.5 + memoryBias / 2) toR++; }
    if (usesMine && r() < fromMine) { fromT++; if (r() < 0.5 - memoryBias / 2) fromR++; }
  }
  return [
    {what: "Actually happened", dir: "Switched to my side", n: toT},
    {what: "Actually happened", dir: "Switched away", n: fromT},
    {what: "What I remember", dir: "Switched to my side", n: toR},
    {what: "What I remember", dir: "Switched away", n: fromR}
  ];
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 220,
  marginLeft: 120,
  fy: {label: null},
  x: {label: "Number of practitioners", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [Plot.barX(foxhole, {fy: "what", y: "dir", x: "n", fill: "dir"}), Plot.ruleX([0])]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const g = (w, d) => foxhole.find(x => x.what === w && x.dir === d).n;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`True net flow toward my side: **${g("Actually happened", "Switched to my side") - g("Actually happened", "Switched away")}**. Remembered net flow: **${g("What I remember", "Switched to my side") - g("What I remember", "Switched away")}**. A selective memory turns two-way traffic into "there are no X's in foxholes."`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- "Everyone agrees with me when it really counts" is a rhetorical move, not evidence.
- Anecdotes about conversions are filtered by who is telling them.
- To judge methods under pressure, look at outcomes, not testimonials.
:::
